purpose: File synchronization service, used to efficiently mirror or back up directories between hosts.
description: The rsync daemon (rsyncd) can be configured with named 'modules' that map to filesystem paths. Modules left without a password, or configured with read/write access for anonymous connections, allow any network client to list, download, or upload arbitrary files under that path.
common_risks: sensitive backups exposed via a listable module
misconfigurations: rsyncd.conf module with no auth users / secrets file configured
read only = false on a module that doesn't need write access
daemon bound to a public interface instead of an internal one
attack_patterns: List available modules with `rsync rsync://target/` and download anything unauthenticated
Upload a malicious file into a writable module (e.g. a web root or cron-executed path)
Pull full backup archives left exposed in a module, exposing credentials or PII
real_world_incidents: Exposed rsync daemons with unauthenticated, writable modules have been used to plant malicious files into web roots and cron-executed directories, leading to remote code execution on the exporting host.
recommended_actions: Require authentication (auth users + secrets file) on every rsyncd module.
Set `read only = true` on any module that doesn't specifically need write access.
Bind rsyncd to an internal interface only, or tunnel over SSH instead of running the standalone daemon.
Firewall port 873 to trusted hosts only.

audience_guidance.student: rsync is a tool for efficiently copying files between computers, and it can run as a background service (a 'daemon') that other computers connect to. If that daemon has no password, anyone can list, download — or in the worst case, upload — files in whatever folder it's sharing.
audience_guidance.developer: Always configure `auth users` and a secrets file for any rsyncd module, and default every module to `read only = true` unless write access is explicitly required.
audience_guidance.bug_bounty_hunter: Run `rsync rsync://target/` with no credentials to list modules — an anonymous listable or writable module is a quick, high-value finding.
audience_guidance.pentester: Download exposed module contents for sensitive data, and if a module is writable, test planting a file into a path that gets executed (web root, cron directory) for RCE.
audience_guidance.security_team: Audit every rsyncd.conf for modules missing authentication or unnecessarily set to writable, and confirm the daemon isn't bound to a public interface.
